articles.title: The messages that run a workplace

body.support:
Every workplace runs on short messages. Each one has a job.

1. **Rosters** say who works when. Find your name. Check the **date** and **times**.
2. **Notices** tell everyone something. The key fact goes first.
3. **Requests** ask for something, like a swap. Say **what**, **when** and **why**. Offer a fix: *Jo can cover.*
4. **Handover notes** tell the next shift what they need. Use: **Done**, **Not done**, **Watch out**.

Good work messages are **short**, **clear**, **polite** and **spelled right**.
body.core:
Every workplace runs on short texts. They're called **organisational texts**, and each has a job.

1. **Rosters** tell you who works when. Find your name, run along the row, and check the **date** and **times**. Read the notes at the bottom too, like *Swaps must be approved by Friday*.
2. **Notices** tell everyone something. Good ones put the key fact first: *The cool room is broken. Don't use it until Monday.*
3. **Requests** ask for something, like a shift swap. A request that gets a yes says **what**, **when** and **why**, and offers a fix: *Jo can cover.*
4. **Handover notes** pass on what the next shift needs. Use three headings: **Done**, **Not done**, **Watch out**.

All good workplace messages are **short**, **specific** (dates, times, names), **polite** and **spelled right**. Save the slang for your mates. A message to your manager is a small piece of your reputation.
body.extend:
Workplaces run on a family of short, practical texts called **organisational texts**. Each has a shape you can recognise, because each does one job.

1. **Rosters** are tables: names down the side, days across the top, times in the cells. The notes at the bottom often hold the rules, like swap deadlines and who approves changes.
2. **Notices** put the key fact first, then the detail and an action.
3. **Requests**, like a shift swap, work when they're specific (what, when, why) and solve the manager's problem for them (*Jo has agreed to cover*).
4. **Handover notes** pass the job from one shift to the next. A reliable shape is **Done / Not done / Watch out**, with names and times.

They all share the same features: short, exact, polite and correctly written. In some workplaces, a vague handover isn't just sloppy. It's dangerous.

caseStudies.title: Piper Alpha: the message that didn't get through

body.support:
**Piper Alpha** was an oil and gas platform in the sea near Scotland. On **6 July 1988**, it blew up. **167 people died.**

That day, workers took a **safety part** off a pump to fix it. They left a note on paper. But the night shift **never saw it**.

That night, another pump broke. The night shift turned on the pump that was being fixed. Gas leaked out and exploded.

An inquiry said the way shifts passed on information **did not work**.

One missing message was part of what went wrong.
body.core:
**Piper Alpha** was an oil and gas platform in the North Sea, off Scotland. On **6 July 1988**, it exploded. **167 people died.**

That day, the day shift took a **safety valve** off one of two pumps for repairs. They covered the hole with a metal plate, but it wasn't tight. The **paperwork** for that job wasn't kept with the paperwork for the pump, so the night shift didn't know the valve was missing.

That night, the other pump broke down. The night shift started the pump that was being repaired. Gas leaked out and exploded.

An inquiry led by **Lord Cullen** found that the system of written permits wasn't working, and that there was no clear way to hand over between shifts. It made **106 recommendations** that changed offshore safety.

One missing piece of information, passed between shifts, was part of what went wrong.
body.extend:
**Piper Alpha** was an oil and gas production platform in the North Sea, off Scotland. On **6 July 1988**, a series of explosions and fires destroyed it. **167 people died.**

During the day shift, a **pressure safety valve** was removed from one of two condensate pumps for maintenance, and the opening was sealed with a blank plate that was not leak-tested. The permit for that valve work was not kept with the permit for the pump itself, so the night shift did not know the valve was missing.

When the second pump failed that night, the crew restarted the pump under repair. Gas escaped and ignited.

The public inquiry led by **Lord Cullen** found that the permit-to-work system was inadequate and routinely departed from, and that there was no clear procedure for shift handover. Its **106 recommendations** reshaped offshore safety regulation.

The disaster had many causes. But it shows, at the highest stakes, that organisational texts — permits, logs, handovers — are only as good as the systems that make sure the right person reads them.

teacher.overview: Students read and write the short organisational texts that run workplaces: rosters, notices, requests and handover notes. They learn each text's structure and characteristics (front-loaded, specific, polite, correct). The case study is the 1988 Piper Alpha disaster, where a shift handover and permit failure was a major contributing cause.
prep: Optional: ask students with jobs to bring (or screenshot, with names removed) a real roster or work group-chat message.
Read the case study first and decide how to frame it (see the reality check).

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Read the roster
steps: **Hook (10 min):** show a real-looking unclear manager text. What would you reply?
**Explicit teaching (10 min):** four organisational texts and their characteristics.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Clear or not?
steps: **Sort (15 min):** would you approve this? Discuss what's missing.
**Case study (25 min):** Piper Alpha; write the handover that should have been left.
**Exit (10 min):** one rule for a good handover.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Write them
steps: **Model (5 min):** write a swap request live.
**Check & reflect (20 min):** Level Up for fast finishers, quick check, reflection, sign-off.

teacher.answers:
**Roster:** Thursday — Jo 4–9. Sunday — Jo and Sam 9–3, so Alex could cover if available (Alex is off). Jo's Thursday is 5 hours, so no break (breaks apply to shifts **over** 5 hours).

**Annotation:** 1 dates/week; 2 roster table; 3 swap rule (Priya, Friday 12 pm); 4 break rule; 5 contact.

**Sort:** cant come tmrw — unclear; sick + Jo can cover — clear; did stuff — unclear; DONE/NOT DONE/WATCH OUT — clear; can I get Saturday — unclear; cool room notice — clear.

**Piper Alpha handover (sample):** DONE: PSV removed from pump A, blank fitted (not leak-tested). NOT DONE: PSV refit. WATCH OUT: do NOT start pump A until the PSV is back and tested.

realityCheck: **The case study is heavy.** 167 people died. Some students may have family who work on mines, rigs or sites. Frame it calmly as a real reason handovers matter, and keep the discussion on systems, not blame.
**It's a lot of industry detail.** Words like condensate pump and permit-to-work can lose students. The support version keeps it simple; with others, sketch the two pumps on the board.
**Students with jobs are gold here.** Real rosters and group-chat messages (names removed) make it authentic. Students without jobs can use the café.
**The roster maths catches people.** “Over 5 hours” vs “5 hours” is a nice close-reading moment; expect debate.
**Works in a real class:** yes. It's short, practical and immediately useful for anyone with a part-time job. It's a good first VM Units 3 & 4 course.
